title: SQL from the JVM: JDBC, pools, batching and migrations
goal: By the end, you can explain what a database connection and each statement cost a program, share a few connections through a pool and find one that was never given back, keep typed-in text out of your SQL, cut thousands of round trips to a handful, spot the hidden loop of queries that a library turning rows into objects (an ORM) can cause, and change a table's columns safely with numbered migrations.
opening:
Picture the payments company at midnight. A small program reads the day's card payments from a partner's file, 2,000 lines, and stores each one in the database. On a laptop it takes two to six seconds. Someone watches the database while it runs, and it's almost idle: it spends a few microseconds on each payment, then waits for the next.

It's easy to think the time goes into the database's work, because that's the part that sounds hard. But the program and the database are two separate programs. Every statement travels from one to the other and waits for its answer, and that trip costs far more than the work.

In JSONB, upserts and MERGE, we typed every statement by hand into psql, PostgreSQL's command-line window. In this lesson, a program sends them. We'll count what a connection costs, share a few connections between many requests, keep a customer's typing out of our SQL, cut 2,000 trips to 2, and change a table's columns without breaking anything. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A program stores 2,000 payments with one INSERT statement (the SQL command that adds a row) at a time, in a loop, all inside one transaction (one group of changes, saved together at the end). The database runs on the same laptop, and one trip there and back takes about half a millisecond. Where does most of the time go?
options: Reading and understanding the INSERT 2,000 times inside the database
Waiting: 2,000 trips there and back, each a send and a wait for the answer, while the database works for microseconds per row
Saving each row to disk, 2,000 times over
Creating 2,000 objects in the program's memory
warmup.why: The loop sends one INSERT and waits for its answer before it sends the next. So 2,000 rows cost 2,000 round trips, a send and a wait each: a second or more, while the database's work per row takes microseconds. One transaction means the rows are saved together once at the end, not 2,000 times. And the INSERT's text is read once and, from the fifth run, kept ready inside the database, as the third section shows. The fourth section sends the same rows in 9 round trips.

sections.h: What a connection costs, and why every statement waits
sections.body:
Let's start with the smallest program that talks to the database. Our payments app keeps its data in PostgreSQL, a free database program, in tables: `merchants` has one row per shop (the labs call a shop a merchant), and `payments` one row per card payment. Programs ask it questions, called queries, in SQL. This lesson's programs are written in Kotlin and run on the JVM, the program that runs Java and Kotlin code. They reach the database through JDBC, the standard library Java and Kotlin use to talk to databases. JDBC needs a driver for each database, a library that speaks that database's language over the network. PostgreSQL's is called pgJDBC.

First, the program opens a connection, an object of type `java.sql.Connection`. Behind it is one network connection to the database's computer, on port 5432 (a port is a number that says which program on a computer a message is for). At the far end, PostgreSQL starts a new server process, a separate running program, for this connection alone. Open ten connections and the database runs ten processes; the first Try it prints their numbers.

Opening a connection is slow by computer standards. Before the first query can run, the driver and the database exchange five rounds of messages (the demo counts them) to agree on the rules and check the password, and the database starts its process. On a laptop that took 12 to 55 ms, thousandths of a second.

Once it's open, every statement is one round trip:

```kotlin
DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/course", "sfz", "sfz").use { conn ->
    conn.prepareStatement("SELECT name FROM merchants WHERE merchant_id = ?").use { ps ->
        ps.setLong(1, 4)
        ps.executeQuery().use { rs ->              // send the statement, block until the answer arrives
            while (rs.next()) println(rs.getString("name"))
        }
    }
}                                                  // use { } closes all three, even after an exception
```

`prepareStatement` holds the SQL, where `?` marks a value we fill in later, and `setLong(1, 4)` puts shop number 4 in its place. `executeQuery` writes the statement onto the connection, and the program stops and waits until the answer comes back. That send-and-wait is a **round trip**. It took 0.3 to 1 ms between two programs on a laptop, through Docker. Between two data centres in the same area it's about a millisecond, and between distant regions about 70 ms. The database's own work to find one row by its key is a few microseconds, millionths of a second. So for small statements, the number of round trips decides how long the work takes.

A post office counter is a fair picture. Opening a connection is opening a new window: someone sets up the desk and checks an ID. A round trip is handing over one form and waiting for the stamp. The clerk stamps in a second, and the waiting is what takes the time.

Two defaults come with every connection. The first is autocommit. A transaction is a group of changes the database saves all together or not at all, and JDBC starts with every statement as its own transaction, saved as soon as it runs. Set `conn.autoCommit = false`, and changes wait until you call `commit()`.

The second is how results arrive. pgJDBC reads the whole result into the program's memory, in one round trip, before `next()`, which steps through the result, returns the first row. A million-row result held 122 MB before our code saw a single row. With autocommit off and `ps.fetchSize = 10_000`, the driver opens a cursor, a bookmark inside the database, and fetches 10,000 rows per round trip instead: about 1 MB held, 101 round trips. Use that for exports and jobs that read a whole big table, not for a query that returns one page.

So a program holds a few connections, each ending in a process on the database, and every statement waits for its answer. Each section cuts one of two counts, connections opened or round trips made. Next, we'll cut the first.

try.title: What a connection costs, and what a query costs
steps: Start the database if it isn't running: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, from the `labs` folder. Docker runs the database in a small, separate Linux system on your laptop, called a container. The demo connects to the database `course` on `localhost:5432`, which means port 5432 on your own computer.

From the `labs` folder, run the demo. It opens ten connections, runs 1,000 `SELECT 1` queries (the smallest query there is) on one connection, borrows from a pool 1,000 times, and reads a million made-up rows twice. A wrapped connection counts the round trips.
Before you run it, predict how many times cheaper a query on an open connection is than opening a new one. Then compare the two memory figures at the end.

try.expect:
One run on a busy laptop (the times move a lot between runs; the counts don't):

```text
open a connection:            median 12.434 ms   (5 round trips each)
  ten connections, ten server processes: 8426 8427 8428 8429 8430 8431 8432 8433 8434 8435
SELECT 1 on an open one:      median 0.482 ms   (1000 round trips for 1,000 queries)
borrow from a pool of 4:      median 0.002 ms
borrow + SELECT 1 + return:   median 0.617 ms
1,000,000 rows, fetchSize 0      heap held at the first row:  122 MB, round trips: 1
1,000,000 rows, fetchSize 10000  heap held at the first row:    1 MB, round trips: 101
```

Across three runs, opening a connection took 12 to 55 ms and a `SELECT 1` 0.3 to 1 ms, so a query on an open connection is 25 to 100 times cheaper than a new connection. Every connection got its own process on the database. Borrowing from a pool, which the next section explains, costs a microsecond or two. The heap is the memory the JVM gives the program's objects. The default fetch held the whole million rows there (122 MB) before the first `next()` returned; the cursor held 1 MB and paid 100 extra round trips for it.

sections.h: Sharing a few open connections: the connection pool
sections.body:
Our program serves many requests at once: each time a shop owner opens the dashboard, that's one request. A request that opens its own connection pays 12 to 55 ms before its first query, and the database starts and stops a process for it. Five hundred requests at once would need 500 processes, and PostgreSQL accepts at most `max_connections` (100 by default) and refuses the rest with an error.

A **connection pool** opens a few connections once and lends them out. HikariCP (Hikari for short), a free pool library that many Java and Kotlin programs use, keeps them in a list. Asking it for one, `dataSource.connection`, hands out an idle connection in about a microsecond. Calling `close()` on a borrowed connection doesn't close it: it gives the connection back, still logged in, to the next borrower. When every connection is lent out, the next borrower waits, for at most `connectionTimeout` (30 seconds by default), and then gets an error, `SQLTransientConnectionException`. The stepper shows a pool of four serving six requests. In the post office picture, the pool keeps four windows open all day and sends each customer to a free one.

How many connections? Fewer than you think. A computer runs one piece of work per CPU core at a time (a core is one of the processor's independent workers, and a laptop has about 8 to 16). With more busy connections than cores, the operating system (the program that runs all the others) takes turns between them, and they fight over the same memory and disk. Each query gets slower, and the total done per second doesn't rise.

Here the post office picture breaks. At a real counter, more windows mean shorter queues. Past a few windows per clerk, a database only gets slower, because every window still feeds the same few clerks, who keep switching between them.

HikariCP's guide on pool sizing starts from connections = (cores × 2) + effective spindles. Spindles are disks, counted only for the reads that memory can't absorb, so that's about 9 for a 4-core database whose data fits in memory. The guide cites a test by Oracle, the company behind another big database, where cutting a pool from 2,048 connections to 96 brought response times from about 100 ms to about 2 ms. Its summary is worth keeping: "You want a small pool, saturated with threads waiting for connections." (A thread is one line of work running inside a program.) The budget is for the whole database, not for each copy of the program: twelve copies with a pool of 20 each put 240 connections on one database.

```kotlin
val pool = HikariDataSource(HikariConfig().apply {
    jdbcUrl = "jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/payments"
    username = "payments"
    password = System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD")
    maximumPoolSize = 10                  // (4 cores x 2) + 0, rounded up: one copy of the program
    connectionTimeout = 2_000             // fail a request after 2 s, not 30
    leakDetectionThreshold = 10_000       // log who has kept a connection for 10 s
})
pool.connection.use { conn -> /* one unit of work */ }
```

The failure to watch for is a leak: code that borrows a connection and never calls `close()`, often on the path taken after an error. Each leak keeps one connection forever. After four, a pool of four is empty, and every request waits `connectionTimeout` and then fails, while the database sits idle. Borrow inside `use { }`, which closes what it holds when its block ends, even after an error. And set `leakDetectionThreshold`, so Hikari prints the code location of whoever held a connection too long.

Connections are cheap now. Next, we'll look at what travels on them, and at a customer who types something unexpected.

sections.h: Keeping typed-in text out of the SQL: prepared statements
sections.body:
Say a shop owner searches for her shop by name. The quick way to build the query is to paste the name into the SQL text: `"SELECT ... WHERE name = '$name'"`, where `$name` inside a Kotlin string inserts the variable. It breaks on the first apostrophe. With `Mama's Kitchen`, the apostrophe ends the quoted name early, and the database reports a syntax error: the text no longer reads as SQL.

With the name `' OR '1'='1`, it's worse. The condition becomes `name = '' OR '1'='1'`, which is true for every row, and the query returns all 8 shops; the Try it shows it. A name that closes the quote and adds `; UPDATE merchants ...`, a second statement that changes rows, makes the database run a statement the attacker wrote. That's **SQL injection**: text from outside that the database reads as SQL.

A `PreparedStatement` takes the possibility away. pgJDBC sends the SQL text with numbered placeholders (`... WHERE name = $1`) in one message, called Parse. It sends the values in a separate message, called Bind, and then asks the database to run the statement (Execute). The database has finished reading the SQL before it receives a single value, so a value can only be compared or stored, whatever characters it contains. The lab stores `Evil Corp', '5999', 'GB') RETURNING merchant_id; UPDATE merchants SET name = 'pwned' ...` as one shop's name, character for character.

In the post office picture, this is a printed form with boxes. Whatever a customer writes in the name box is read as a name, never as an instruction to the clerk.

```kotlin
conn.prepareStatement("SELECT merchant_id, name FROM merchants WHERE name = ?").use { ps ->
    ps.setString(1, name)                  // a value, never SQL
    ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> /* ... */ }
}
```

Placeholders work for values only. A table name, a column name or a sort direction can't be a `?`. Pick those from a fixed list in your code, `if (dir == "desc") "DESC" else "ASC"`, never straight from the request.

The split pays a second time. From the fifth run of the same PreparedStatement object (pgJDBC's `prepareThreshold`, 5 by default), the driver gives the statement a name inside the database, `S_1` in the Try it, and later runs skip reading the SQL again. Named statements belong to their connection, so a pool that keeps its connections open keeps them ready.

Inserts often need the new row's id, the number the database gave it. In SQL that's `INSERT ... RETURNING merchant_id`. Through JDBC, name the id column: `conn.prepareStatement(sql, arrayOf("merchant_id"))`, then read `ps.generatedKeys`. The flag `Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS` does different things on different drivers. pgJDBC adds `RETURNING *` and sends back every column of the new row, while Oracle's driver returns an internal row address, the ROWID, instead of the id.

Values are safe now. But 2,000 payments are still 2,000 round trips. Next, we'll send them together.

sections.h: Fewer round trips: batches, and the N+1 queries an ORM can hide
sections.body:
Back to the opening's midnight import, which inserts 2,000 payments with a PreparedStatement and `executeUpdate()` in a loop. The Try it counts the cost: 2,000 round trips, 2,000 INSERT statements on the database, 1.6 to 6 seconds on a laptop. The database spends microseconds on each row. Nearly all of the time is the driver waiting for answers.

`addBatch()` puts a row in a queue inside the driver instead of sending it, and `executeBatch()` sends the queue. pgJDBC writes the INSERTs onto the connection one after another without waiting, and stops to read the answers only when enough of them have piled up: 9 round trips for 2,000 rows, about a tenth of a second. The database still runs 2,000 statements. In the post office picture, that's one envelope holding all the forms.

Add `reWriteBatchedInserts=true` to the connection settings, and the driver also rewrites the batch into INSERTs of many rows each, `INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...), ...`. Then 2,000 rows become 6 statements, of 1,024, 512, 256, 128, 64 and 16 rows, in 2 round trips. pgJDBC's documentation claims 2 to 3 times the speed for that rewrite. For millions of rows, `COPY`, through pgJDBC's `CopyManager`, streams everything as one statement.

```kotlin
conn.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO payments (card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)").use { ps ->
    for (p in rows) {
        ps.setLong(1, p.cardId)            // ... and the other four
        ps.addBatch()                      // queued in the driver, nothing sent
    }
    ps.executeBatch()                      // sent together
}
```

Reads have the same trap, and it often hides inside an ORM. Writing JDBC code for every table gets tedious, so many programs use an object-relational mapper (ORM), a library that turns rows into objects and back. Hibernate is the best-known one for Java, and Exposed is a Kotlin library with an ORM part. You write a class, `Merchant`, and the ORM maps it to a table, each field to a column, and each object to the row with its primary key, the column that names each row. A field such as `payment.merchant` maps to a foreign key, a column that holds another row's key. The ORM follows it with a join (a query that combines rows of two tables), or with one more query the first time the field is read, which is called lazy loading.

Objects and tables are two shapes for the same facts, and the gap between them is called the **object-relational mismatch**. The mapping leaks in three places. Code walks objects one reference at a time, while SQL answers whole sets of rows, so a loop over objects becomes a loop of queries. The ORM keeps one object per row for each piece of work (an identity map), so asking for the same row again returns the copy it already holds, even after another program changed the row. And SQL's rules still apply under the objects: `reason = ?` given a missing value, NULL, matches nothing, because NULL compared with anything is unknown.

The first leak is the one to measure. The shop dashboard loads the 8 shops and then, for each one, reads `merchant.latestPayment`, which a lazy-loading ORM fetches with one more query. That's the **N+1 query** pattern: one query for the list, then one per row. Eight shops cost 9 round trips; the 2,500 shops of the large data set would cost 2,501. Each query is fast, so none of them looks slow. What gives it away is `pg_stat_statements`, a PostgreSQL add-on that counts every statement the database runs: it shows the per-shop query with a huge `calls` count and a tiny average time.

The fix moves the loop into the database. Write one query with `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... LIMIT 1`, which runs the small per-shop query inside the database (LATERAL joins, top-N per group and keyset pagination built it). Or write two: the shops, then all their payments at once with `WHERE merchant_id = ANY (?)`, bound to an array (a list) of ids, which is what an ORM's batch fetching sends. The figure counts the round trips of all five versions.

What's left is a safe way to change the tables themselves. Next, we'll meet it.

aside.title: So should I avoid ORMs?
aside.body: No. An ORM saves a lot of repetitive code, and most of the queries it sends are fine. Treat it as a tool that writes SQL for you, and check what it writes. Count the queries a page sends in a test, as this lesson's lab does, and fetch related rows together when the count grows with the data: Hibernate calls that `JOIN FETCH`, and Exposed uses `with()`. When a query is easier to say in SQL, write it in SQL.

sections.h: Changing a table's shape safely: numbered migrations
sections.body:
So far every table already existed. But programs change, and their tables must change with them. The lab's payouts program, which records the money paid out to each shop, needs a new `status` column. A statement that changes a table's shape, such as `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`, is called DDL (data definition language). And the same tables live in several places: each developer's laptop, the test machines, a practice copy and the real one. Each needs the same changes, in the same order, exactly once, and a person typing them by hand will miss one.

A migration tool keeps the history of those changes inside the database itself. Flyway, a free migration tool for Java and Kotlin programs, reads SQL files named by version from a folder, `V1__create_payouts.sql`, `V2__payout_status.sql`, and keeps a table of its own, `flyway_schema_history`, with one row per applied version. Each row holds the version, a description, the file name, a checksum and whether it succeeded. A checksum is a number worked out from every character of a file, so any change to the file changes the number. `migrate()` compares the folder with the table and runs the files the table doesn't list yet, in version order, each in its own transaction on PostgreSQL. It records each one as it succeeds, and on a database that's up to date it does nothing.

```kotlin
Flyway.configure()
    .dataSource(url, user, password)
    .locations("classpath:db/migration")
    .load()
    .migrate()                             // at start-up, before the program takes requests
```

Before it runs anything, Flyway validates. If an applied file has changed, even by one comment, its checksum (Flyway uses one called CRC32) no longer matches the history, and `migrate()` stops: `Migration checksum mismatch for migration version 2`. So **never edit an applied migration**. The real database ran the old text; fix forward with a V3.

In PostgreSQL, DDL is transactional, so a migration that fails halfway leaves nothing behind: the new column, every other change and the history row roll back together. (Oracle's database saves each DDL statement on its own, so a failed migration there can leave half its changes behind.) The lab's migration fails the classic way. `ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL` works on the empty database of every test run, and fails on the real one, where the existing payouts have no status. `NOT NULL` is a rule that the column must hold a value, and the error is 23502. A DEFAULT, a value PostgreSQL fills in when none is given, fixes it, and since PostgreSQL 11 a constant default doesn't rewrite the whole table. Test migrations on tables that have rows.

A migration that runs while the program keeps serving customers needs one more rule. While a new version rolls out, the old and the new version of the program both run against the new tables, so a change such as renaming a column goes in steps, each safe for both versions. The Encoding track's lesson Data outlives code: rolling upgrades and migrations builds that pattern, called expand and contract.

Libraries such as jOOQ (3.21), which builds Kotlin or Java classes from the tables, and Exposed (1.6), JetBrains' Kotlin library for SQL, sit on top of JDBC. They borrow connections from a pool and send statements over the same round trips, so everything in this lesson applies to them.

That's also the limit of this track. Every lesson used a database someone else had set up, on one machine, with tables as the only shape for data. Running PostgreSQL: processes, configuration, roles and connections, in the Storage engines track, opens up the server. PostgreSQL replication, backups and failover puts copies on other machines. And the next track asks whether tables are the right shape at all.

compare.note: Oracle Database, a commercial database program that many banks run, has its own JDBC driver. The JDBC calls are the same, but the two drivers' defaults point in opposite directions. Oracle's driver fetches results in small slices by default, 10 rows per round trip, so a large report makes thousands of round trips until you raise the fetch size. pgJDBC loads the whole result at once, so a large report runs out of memory until you turn autocommit off and set a fetch size. For new ids, name the id column on both: it's the only form that returns the id on both drivers, and the column name follows each database's rule for capital letters. Oracle's driver sends a batch together without any setting; pgJDBC needs reWriteBatchedInserts to turn it into a few statements.

worked.title: An importer for 50,000 payments: pooled, batched, in chunks, and safe to rerun

steps.say: The importer runs inside a program that already has a pool. Its settings come from the formula and from this job's needs: the database has 4 cores, and the batches should be rewritten into INSERTs of many rows.

One batch of 50,000 rows would be one long transaction, holding its locks (the database's marks that keep others off the rows being changed) until the end, and one bad row would lose everything. Chunks of 1,000 rows, each its own transaction, keep each save small. Each chunk costs a few round trips instead of 1,000.

A crash after chunk 23 means the job runs again from the start. The partner's file carries each payment's code, `payment_uid`, so the INSERT skips rows that are already there, as in JSONB, upserts and MERGE. Rerunning the whole file is now harmless, and the batch rewrite still works for `ON CONFLICT` inserts.

INSERT INTO payments (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)

FROM pg_stat_statements

lab.title: A safe lookup, a pool, a batch, one query instead of N+1, and a migration
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the `labs` folder. Tests are small programs that check your code against a real PostgreSQL. Twelve of the twenty fail for now. They count round trips through a wrapped connection (`support/RoundTrips.kt`) and statements with `pg_stat_statements`, so they pass or fail the same way on a fast or a slow machine.
`MerchantRepository.kt` pastes names into SQL. Rewrite `create` and `findByName` with `?` placeholders. The tests store `Mama's Kitchen` and an injection attempt as names, and look up `' OR '1'='1`.

`PaymentLoader.kt` has two parts. Fill in `poolConfig`: 4 connections, a 2-second `connectionTimeout`, `reWriteBatchedInserts`, and the pool name `importer`. Then turn the loop in `insertPayments` into one batch, and return the number of rows inserted.
`MerchantReport.kt` builds the shop dashboard with N+1 queries. Make it one or two round trips with the same results, including the two shops that have no payment.

`V2__payout_status.sql` passes on an empty database and fails on a table with rows. The tests run Flyway on a fresh schema each time, including one that applies V1, adds payouts, then applies V2. Fix V2 (never V1), and run the tests until all twenty pass.

With the rewrite on, `executeBatch()` reports `Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO` (-2) for each row instead of 1, meaning "it worked, but I can't say how many rows". Count those as one row each.

One query: `FROM merchants m LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE merchant_id = m.merchant_id AND status = 'succeeded' ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC LIMIT 1) p ON true ORDER BY m.merchant_id`. A shop with no payment gets NULL ids: read them with `getLong` and then `wasNull()`, or with `getObject`.
`ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (...)`: the default fills the existing rows, and every new row that names no status.

drill.title: Borrow, batch, commit, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write a Kotlin function `saveAll(pool: DataSource, rows: List<Refund>)` that borrows a connection, inserts all the refunds (`payment_id`, `amount_minor`, `reason`, `created_at`) in one batch inside one transaction, commits, rolls back on any `SQLException` (JDBC's error type), and always gives the connection back. Then name the connection setting that turns the batch into INSERTs of many rows.

recap: A JDBC connection is a network connection with its own process on the database. Opening one took 5 round trips and 12 to 55 ms here. After that, every statement is a round trip, and for small statements the number of round trips decides the time.

A pool opens a few connections once and lends them out, and `close()` gives one back. Size it near (cores × 2) + spindles for the whole database, keep `connectionTimeout` short, borrow inside `use { }`, and let `leakDetectionThreshold` find leaks.
A PreparedStatement sends the SQL and the values in separate messages, so a value can never become SQL. Table and column names come from a fixed list in your code. Ask for new ids by column name.

`addBatch` and `executeBatch` turn 2,000 round trips into 9, and `reWriteBatchedInserts=true` also turns 2,000 INSERTs into 6. An ORM's lazy loading can hide N+1 queries: replace them with a join, LATERAL or one `= ANY (?)` query, and find them by `calls` in `pg_stat_statements`.
Flyway runs numbered scripts in order and records each with a checksum in `flyway_schema_history`. Never edit an applied migration, and test migrations on tables that have rows.

The limit: all of this assumed one database on one machine, set up by someone else, with tables as the only shape for data. What's inside the server, copies on other machines and other shapes of data come in later tracks.
closing:
We started with a midnight import that took seconds while the database sat idle. The time went into 2,000 round trips, and a batch cut them to 2. A pool, placeholders and numbered migrations took care of the rest.

You can watch round trips in any web browser. Open its developer tools (F12 in most browsers), choose the Network tab and load a page: each line is one request and its wait. A page that sends forty small requests for one list has the N+1 pattern, one level up.

That ends the SQL track. Next, the Data models track asks what tables make hard, and why anyone would store data in another shape.

quiz.q: A payments program runs as 12 copies, each with a Hikari pool of 50, against one 8-core PostgreSQL database whose data fits in memory. Under load the database shows hundreds of busy connections, and every query is slow. What do you change first?
options: Raise max_connections and give each copy 100 connections
Shrink the pools so all copies together hold a few dozen connections, near (8 × 2) + 0, and let requests wait in the pools
Set connectionTimeout to 0 so no request ever waits for a connection
Open a new connection per request so the pool can't run dry
quiz.why: The database can run about 8 queries at once, one per core. Six hundred connections that all want a core make every query wait for the processor, memory and locks, so each one is slower and the total done per second falls. A small total, with requests waiting in the pools, keeps the database busy without the switching; that's the HikariCP guide's point. More connections make it worse, and a new connection per request adds the login cost to every request.

quiz.q: A web page lets the caller choose the column to sort by, and the code pastes it in: `"SELECT ... FROM payments ORDER BY $sort"`. How do you make it safe?
options: Bind it: `ORDER BY ?` with `ps.setString(1, sort)`
Escape single quotes in `sort` before pasting it
Map the request value to one of a fixed set of column names in code, and reject anything else
Run the query on a read-only connection
quiz.why: A placeholder carries a value, not a column name: `ORDER BY ?` sorts by one fixed piece of text, the same for every row, so nothing gets sorted. Escaping quotes doesn't help, because a column name needs no quotes to carry an attack (`created_at; DROP TABLE ...`). A read-only connection limits the damage, but still lets a caller read what they shouldn't. Pick names from a fixed list.

quiz.q: The import program now uses `addBatch` and `executeBatch` for 10,000 rows, and its time dropped a lot. Yet `pg_stat_statements` still shows `calls = 10000` for its INSERT. Why?
options: The batch is not working: autocommit sends each row on its own
A batch saves round trips, not statements: pgJDBC still sends one INSERT per row. `reWriteBatchedInserts=true` turns them into a few multi-row INSERTs
pg_stat_statements counts rows, not statements
PostgreSQL splits every batch back into single rows
quiz.why: pgJDBC writes the queued INSERTs back to back and reads the answers only when its buffer fills, so 10,000 statements cost a handful of round trips, which is where the time went. The database still runs each one. With the rewrite setting, the driver builds INSERTs with many rows each, and calls drops to a few dozen. pg_stat_statements reports calls and rows separately.

quiz.q: LATERAL joins, top-N per group and keyset pagination built LATERAL joins. The shop dashboard loads the shops, then runs one query per shop for its latest succeeded payment: N+1. Which single query keeps every shop, including those with no payment?
options: `FROM merchants m CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ... LIMIT 1) p`
`FROM merchants m JOIN payments p ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 1`
`FROM merchants m LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE merchant_id = m.merchant_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC LIMIT 1) p ON true`
`FROM merchants m LEFT JOIN payments p USING (merchant_id) GROUP BY m.merchant_id`
quiz.why: LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true runs the subquery once per shop inside the database, and keeps shops whose subquery returned nothing, with NULLs. CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops them. The LIMIT 1 outside the join returns one row for the whole query. And GROUP BY alone can't return the other columns of the latest payment.

quiz.q: A teammate fixes a typo in a comment inside `V7__refund_index.sql`, which the real database applied last month, and ships the change. The program runs Flyway's `migrate()` when it starts. What happens?
options: Nothing: comments don't change the tables
Flyway runs V7 again, and fails because the index exists
Flyway reports a checksum mismatch for version 7 and stops, so the program doesn't start
Flyway applies the new comment as version 8
quiz.why: Flyway stores each applied script's checksum and checks it before migrating. The edited file's checksum differs, so migrate fails with `Migration checksum mismatch for migration version 7`. It never reruns an applied version and never invents a new one. Undo the edit; if the change was meant, a new V8 is the way to ship it.

flashcards.front: What does `close()` do on a connection borrowed from a pool?
flashcards.back: Gives it back to the pool, still open and logged in. The network connection and the database's process stay.
How long `getConnection()` waits for a free connection before throwing SQLTransientConnectionException. Default 30 seconds.

flashcards.front: The HikariCP guide's starting point for pool size?
flashcards.back: connections = (cores × 2) + effective spindles, for the whole database. About 9 for 4 cores and data that fits in memory.

flashcards.front: Why can't a value bound to a PreparedStatement become SQL?
flashcards.back: The driver sends the SQL text (Parse) and the values (Bind) in separate messages; the database has read the SQL before it sees any value.

flashcards.front: addBatch alone vs reWriteBatchedInserts: what does each cut?
flashcards.back: addBatch cuts round trips (2,000 rows: 9). The rewrite also cuts statements, into INSERTs of many rows (2,000 rows: 6).

flashcards.front: In one Hibernate session (one unit of work), you load shop 4, another program renames it and commits, and you call `find` again. Which name do you see?
flashcards.back: The old one. The session is an identity map: it returns the object it already holds without asking the database. `refresh()` or a new session reads the new name.

flashcards.front: Why must you never edit an applied Flyway migration?
flashcards.back: Flyway stored its checksum, so the next migrate fails with a checksum mismatch. Fix forward with a new version.

terms.plain: One send-and-wait between the program and the database: the driver sends a request, then waits until the answer arrives.
A set of open, logged-in connections that the program borrows and gives back, instead of opening one per request.
A borrowed connection that is never given back; enough of them empty the pool.
SQL with placeholders whose values travel separately from the text, so they are never read as SQL.
Text from outside, pasted into SQL, that the database reads as SQL and that changes what the statement does.
A library that turns rows into objects and back. The gap between the two shapes, where its mapping leaks, is the object-relational mismatch.
One query for a list, then one more query for each row of it, often from lazy loading in an ORM.
A numbered script that changes the tables, applied once per database and recorded in a history table.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate's import program inserts 10,000 rows with `executeUpdate()` in a loop. It takes about 10 seconds while the database's processor is almost idle. Explain where the time goes and the two changes that fix it, and how you'd prove the fix in a test without timing it.
explain_back.answer: Each executeUpdate sends one INSERT and waits until the database's answer comes back, so 10,000 rows are 10,000 round trips. At about a millisecond each, that's 10 seconds of waiting, while the database spends microseconds per row, which is why its processor is idle. The first fix is addBatch for each row and one executeBatch: the driver writes the INSERTs back to back and reads the answers only when its buffer fills, so the same rows go in a few dozen round trips. The second is reWriteBatchedInserts=true on the connection or the pool: the driver turns the batch into INSERTs of many rows, so the database runs a few dozen statements instead of 10,000. I'd put both in one transaction, or one per chunk of a few thousand rows. To prove it without a stopwatch, count. Wrap the driver's connection and count the switches from writing to reading, or reset pg_stat_statements and read the INSERT's calls. The loop shows 10,000 of both; the fixed version a few dozen round trips and a few dozen statements, on any machine.

deeper.body:
Why 9 round trips for a batch of 2,000, and not 1? pgJDBC could write all 2,000 INSERTs and only then read the answers. But if the database's answers filled the network buffers (the memory that holds bytes on their way) while the driver was still writing, both sides would wait for each other forever. So the driver estimates how many bytes of answers are waiting, and stops to read them when the estimate passes its limit. That's a few hundred plain INSERTs per round trip. The rewritten INSERTs carry hundreds of rows each, so far fewer answers come back, and 2 round trips do.

PostgreSQL has a 5 of its own, unrelated to pgJDBC's `prepareThreshold`. A named prepared statement is planned with the actual values for its first five runs (custom plans). After that the database may switch to one generic plan for every value, if its estimated cost isn't much worse. A query whose best plan depends on the value can get slower after the fifth run: say a `status` where almost every row is `succeeded` and a few are `pending`. `plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan` turns the switch off for a session or a user.

Connection poolers that sit between many programs and the database, such as PgBouncer in transaction mode, hand each transaction to whichever database connection is free. Anything that lives on a connection between transactions then breaks: session advisory locks, `SET` without `LOCAL`, and named prepared statements, unless the pooler tracks them (PgBouncer does since version 1.21, with `max_prepared_statements`). If you sit behind one, check which of those your driver and code rely on.

Flyway 13 needs two libraries for PostgreSQL, `org.flywaydb:flyway-core` and `org.flywaydb:flyway-database-postgresql`, because support for each database lives in its own module. jOOQ can generate its classes from the tables Flyway built, so a query that names a dropped column stops compiling.

Flyway takes a lock before it migrates, so two copies of a program starting at once don't both apply V3. On PostgreSQL that lock is held in a transaction by default. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which builds an index without blocking writes and can't run inside a transaction, waits for every older transaction to end, including Flyway's own, and so it waits forever: the migration hangs. Put it in a migration of its own and set Flyway's `postgresql.transactional.lock=false`, as the Flyway PostgreSQL page describes.

Virtual threads (JDK 21 and later) make it cheap to run thousands of request threads, and change nothing about the pool. A thousand virtual threads and a pool of ten means 990 threads parked in `getConnection()`, which is exactly the small, saturated pool the HikariCP guide asks for, as long as `connectionTimeout` is short enough to turn requests away instead of piling them up.
